tip: After 'essere' the participle agrees with the subject: a woman 'è scesa' (feminine), a man 'è sceso'. 'Scendere' gives 'sceso'.
'Ci' (there) attaches to the end of a let's-form: 'andiamo' plus 'ci' becomes 'andiamoci' = let's go there.
'Bere' keeps its older stem 'bev-' in the 'imperfetto': 'bevevo' = I used to drink.
Many weather phrases use 'fare' (to make): 'faceva molto caldo' = it was very hot. Also 'fare freddo' for cold.
'Sembra che' (it seems that) flips the following verb to the subjunctive: 'capiscano', not 'capiscono'.
Many verbs of motion take 'essere', and the participle shows who moved: 'è corsa' means a woman ran, 'corso' for a man.
Negative 'tu' commands use 'non' plus the infinitive: 'non aprire', not the normal command form 'apri'.
The 'imperfetto' describes an ongoing background: 'passavamo le sere' means 'we used to spend the evenings', a habit rather than a single event.
'Riposarsi' is reflexive: literally 'rest oneself', so 'ti riposi' keeps the 'ti' where English just says 'you rest'.
Italian uses 'avere' (to have) for this feeling: 'aveva paura' = was afraid, literally had fear.
'Vorrei' is the conditional of 'volere' and softens a request: 'vorrei un caffè' = I would like a coffee.
'Sempre' here signals a past habit, so the verb goes 'imperfetto': 'portava sempre' means 'she always wore'.
When two pronouns stack, indirect comes before direct: 've lo' means 'it to you', both sitting before 'ripeto'.
English 'I preferred' is simple past, but an ongoing preference needs the 'imperfetto' in Italian: 'preferivo'.
'Passato prossimo' ('è arrivata') for event + 'imperfetto' ('scappava') for ongoing action.
Plural reflexive pronouns can mean each other, not just oneself: 'ci chiamiamo' means we call each other.
Negative commands to one person ('tu') use 'non' plus the infinitive: 'non scrivere' means don't write.
Reflexive verbs use reflexive pronouns ('mi', 'ti', 'si', 'ci', 'vi', 'si') before the conjugated verb: 'mi sveglio' (I wake up).
Present tense plus 'da' expresses duration: 'abita' plus 'da tre anni' means he has been living for three years, still ongoing.
'Passato prossimo' ('siamo usciti') for event + 'imperfetto' ('faceva') for background description.
Many weather phrases use 'fare', not 'essere': 'fa freddo' means it is cold, literally it makes cold.
'Voglio che' (I want that) forces the subjunctive: 'mangino', not 'mangiano'.
'Bisogna che' (it's necessary that) forces the subjunctive: 'io faccia', not 'faccio'.
'Passato prossimo' ('l'ho incontrata') for event + 'imperfetto' ('portava') for description.
'Sembra che' (it seems that) triggers the subjunctive on the next verb: 'cambi', not 'cambia'.
'Bisogna che' states a real need, but the action stays hypothetical, so it takes the subjunctive: 'migliori', not 'migliora'.
With an infinitive, the reflexive 'si' attaches to the end: 'lavarsi' means 'to wash oneself'.
Italian usually drops subject pronouns; 'lui' and 'io' appear here for contrast: 'lui studiava' means HE studied, while I slept.
With reflexive verbs and body parts, Italian uses the article, not a possessive: 'si lava le mani' = washes his hands.
Singular family members usually drop the article after a possessive: 'mia madre', not 'la mia madre'.
